::: center
**Handout 26\
Bootstrap Confidence Intervals**
:::

The value of any statistic varies from sample to sample. Statistical
inference procedures such as confidence intervals are based on sampling
distributions which describe how the values of a statistic vary from
sample to sample over many possible samples. In particular, the standard
error of a statistic measures its degree of sample-to-sample
variability.

If a population distribution is assumed, then we can approximate the
sampling distribution of a statistic and characteristics like SE via
simulation. But what if the population distribution is completely
unknown? For some statistics --- most notably means, proportions and
certain transformations --- the Central Limit Theorems and its relatives
(e.g., Delta Method) guarantee that the sampling distribution will be
approximately Normal for large samples, regardless of the population
distribution. However, not every statistic has an approximate Normal
distribution, so we need other methods for approximating sampling
distributions. But how do we estimate the sampling distribution of a
statistic based only on sample data? Bootstrapping provides a simple but
extremely versatile and powerful method for doing so.

::: exer
**Exercise 1**. For purposes of illustration, we'll start with a small
data set. The table below contains data on all the quidditch matches
(for which the final score was discernible) in the *Harry Potter*
books[^1]. The sample mean is $\bar{x}=340$ and the sample SD is
$s=145.6$ points. Say we want a confidence interval for the population
mean score based on this sample
$$200 \qquad 230 \qquad 250 \qquad 260 \qquad 380 \qquad 470 \qquad 590$$
:::

1.  Warmup exercise: If we assume that quidditch scores follow a
    $N(340, 135)$ distribution, explain how you would use simulation to
    approximate the sampling distribution of the sample mean. Note: we
    really want to approximate the sampling distribution without
    assuming anything about the population distribution; this is just to
    remind you of how we have done things so far.

    **Solution:**

    -   Simulate a sample of size $n=7$ from a $N(340, 135)$
        distribution

    -   Compute the sample mean of the simulated values

    -   Repeat many times, recording the sample mean for each simulated
        sample\

2.  How could you estimate the SE of the sample mean based on the above
    simulation? Compare to the theoretical formula.

    **Solution:** The standard deviation of the simulated sample means
    approximates the SE. This should be close to $135/\sqrt{7} = 51$.\

3.  Now suppose we make no assumptions about the population
    distribution. How could you estimate the population distribution
    based on the observed data? Construct a spinner corresponding to
    this distribution.

    **Solution:** Estimate the population distribution with the
    distribution of values in the sample! So the corresponding spinner
    would be divided into 7 equal sectors, one for each of the observed
    values: 200, 230, 250, 260, 380, 470, 590

4.  Continuing the previous part, explain how you would use simulation
    to approximate the sampling distribution of the sample mean *without
    knowing the population distribution*.

    **Solution:** Assuming the sample is representative of the
    population, we can approximate the population distribution with the
    distribution of values in the sample. So we simulate a sample using
    the spinner from the previous part.

    -   *Spin the spinner labeled with the 7 observed values 7 times to
        simulate a single sample*

    -   Compute the sample mean of the simulated values

    -   Repeat many times, recording the sample mean for each simulated
        sample\

5.  Suppose that instead of using a spinner, you wrote each observed
    value on a piece of paper. How would you use the pieces of paper to
    simulate a sample?

    **Solution:** Write each of the 7 observed values on a slip of
    paper: 200, 230, 250, 260, 380, 470, 590. Shuffle the papers and
    deal one; that represents a single simulated value. To simulate a
    sample of size 7, select a sample of size 7 *with replacement* from
    the papers.\

6.  Conduct by hand a few repetitions of the simulation from the
    previous part.

7.  Use software to perform the simulation. How would you use the
    simulation results to approximate the SE? Compare to the usual
    formula; hint: what is the "population" SD?

    **Solution:** The standard deviation of the simulated sample means
    approximates the SE. This should be close to $134.8/\sqrt{7}=51$. We
    are treating the 7 observed values as if they were the population we
    are sampling from. So the "population" distribution takes possible
    values 200, 230, $\ldots$, 590 each with probability $1/7$. The
    "population" mean is $200(1/7) + 230(1/7)+\cdots+590(1/7) = 340$ and
    the "population" variance is
    $$(200-340)^2(1/7) + (230-340)^2(1/7)+\cdots+(590-340)^2(1/7) = 18171$$
    and the "population" SD is $\sqrt{18171} = 134.8$. When sampling
    from a "population" with SD 134.8, the SE of sample means is
    $134.8/\sqrt{7}=51$. (Remember, the sample SD $s$ divides by $n-1=6$
    instead of $n=7$, which is the difference between 134.8 and
    $s=145.6$.)\

8.  How could you find a confidence interval for the population mean?

    **Solution:** Based on the simulation results, the sample-to-sample
    distribution of the sample mean is approximately Normal and the SE
    is about 51. So we could use the usual observed statistic $\pm$ 2 SE
    formula for a 95% confidence interval. The observed sample mean is
    $\bar{x}=340$, so the 95% has endpoints $340\pm 2 \times 51$:
    $[238, 442]$.

-   The sampling distribution of a statistic can be approximated by
    simulating many samples *from the population* and computing the
    value of the statistic for each simulated sample.

-   The idea behind **bootstrapping** is that if the sample data is
    representative of the population, then we can approximate the
    process of selecting a sample from the population by *treating the
    observed sample as if it were the population and selecting a sample
    --- called a resample or bootstrap sample --- from the observed
    sample.*

-   A **bootstrap sample** *resamples* the data from the *observed
    sample*, drawing the same number of observations, but *with
    replacement*.

-   The **bootstrap distribution** of a statistic is obtained by
    simulating many bootstrap samples and computing the value of the
    statistic for each sample

    -   Simulate a (re)sample of size $n$ with replacement from the
        observed sample

    -   Compute the value of the statistic for the simulated bootstrap
        sample

    -   Repeat many times, recording the value of the statistic for each
        repetition

-   The **bootstrap standard error** of a statistic is the standard
    deviation of the bootstrap distribution of the statistic.

-   The bootstrap distribution of a statistic approximates some, but not
    all, features of the sampling distribution of the statistic.

    -   The shape of the bootstrap distribution usually approximates the
        shape of the sampling distribution

    -   The variability of the bootstrap distribution usually
        approximates the variability of the sampling distribution. That
        is, the bootstrap SE usually approximates the true SE.

    -   The center of the bootstrap distribution does NOT accurately
        approximate the center of the sampling distribution

    -   The bootstrap estimate of bias usually approximates the bias of
        the statistic.

-   There are many methods for constructing bootstrap confidence
    intervals for parameters; we'll only study a few.

    -   Normal method: If the bootstrap distribution for the
        corresponding statistic is approximately Normal, then an
        approximate 95% confidence interval has endpoints
        $$\text{observed statistic} \pm 2 \times \text{SE}$$

    -   The 95% **bootstrap percentile interval** is the interval with
        endpoints equal to the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the
        bootstrap distribution.

-   One of the main advantages of bootstrapping is that it can be used
    to approximate the SE of *any statistic*.\

::: exer
**Exercise 2**. Continuing the previous exercise, say we want to
estimate the population *median* quidditch score.
:::

1.  Describe in detail how would use simulation to approximate the
    bootstrap distribution. Then conduct the simulation. What are the
    possible values in the bootstrap distribution? Why?

    **Solution:** Bootstrap simulation works the same as before. The
    only difference is that now for every bootstrap sample you compute
    the sample median rather than the sample mean. Since the sample only
    has 7 values, the sample median will be the middle value after the
    simulated values are arranged in order. That is, the median will
    always be one of the 7 observed values.

2.  Which bootstrap confidence interval would be more appropriate,
    Normal or percentile? Find and interpret the appropriate confidence
    interval.

    **Solution:** Since the median of bootstrap samples takes only 7
    possible values, the bootstrap distribution of the median will be
    very discrete and a Normal approximation will not be valid. But we
    can still find the percentile interval: We estimate with 95%
    confidence that the population median quidditch score is between 230
    and 470 points. (Note: if the sample size were larger, the bootstrap
    distribution of the sample median would be more continuous and a
    Normal approximation might be valid.)

::: exer
**Exercise 3**. Do newborns from mothers who smoke tend to weigh less at
birth than newborns from mothers who don't smoke? The following
summarizes data on a sample of cases in North Carolina over a one year
period.

![image](C:/Users/kjross/Documents/Handout_graphs/babysmoke.png){width="50%"}
:::

1.  Are the above summaries enough information to perform bootstrap
    analyses?

    **Solution:** No. While for procedures like $t$, $F$, etc summary
    statistics are enough, bootstrap methods require the entire sample
    data set.\

2.  Describe in detail how you would use bootstrapping to find a
    confidence interval for the *difference in population means*. Then
    conduct the simulation and find and interpret the confidence
    interval.

    **Solution:** We want the bootstrap distribution of the difference
    in sample means. We assume that we have two independent samples. One
    bootstrap repetition consists of

    -   Select a bootstrap sample of size 873 with replacement from the
        birthweights of babies of non-smokers.

    -   Select a bootstrap sample of size 126 with replacement from the
        birthweights of babies of smokers.

    -   Find the mean birthweight of the simulated non-smoker sample,
        the mean birthweight of the simulated smoker sample, and the
        difference in means (non-smokers $-$ smokers).

    We estimate with 95% confidence that the population mean birthweight
    is between 0.06 to 0.58 *pounds* larger for babies of non-smokers
    than for babies of smokers.

3.  Describe in detail how you would use bootstrapping to find a
    confidence interval for the *ratio of population medians*. Then
    conduct the simulation and find and interpret the confidence
    interval.

    **Solution:** Similar to the previous part but the statistic is the
    ratio of sample medians. We estimate with 95% confidence that the
    population *median* birthweight is between 1 to 1.08 *times* larger
    for babies of non-smokers than for babies of smokers.

::: exer
**Exercise 4**. The scatterplot below displays data on length (feet) and
jaw width (inches) for a sample of sharks.

![image](C:/Users/kjross/Documents/Handout_graphs/shark-scatter){width="30%"}
:::

1.  Describe in detail how you would use bootstrapping to find a
    confidence interval for the *population correlation coefficient*.
    Then conduct the simulation and find and interpret the confidence
    interval.

    **Solution:** The population distribution is now the *joint*
    distribution of jaw width and length. We approximate sampling from
    this joint distribution by resampling from the sample data in which
    each shark has an $(x, y)$ pair. We select a bootstrap sample by
    resampling *pairs* with replacement. Another way to think about it:
    label the sharks from 1 to 44, and then select a sample of 44 labels
    with replacement to be the sharks in the bootstrap sample, and use
    the (jaw width, length) pairs for these sharks.

    For each bootstrap sample, find the sample correlation. Then repeat
    many times.

    We estimate with 95% confidence that the population correlation
    between length and jaw width of sharks is between 0.79 and 0.93.

::: exer
**Exercise 5**. Consider again the quidditch data
$$200 \qquad 230 \qquad 250 \qquad 260 \qquad 380 \qquad 470 \qquad 590$$
:::

1.  What is the center of the *sampling distribution* of the sample
    mean? Why? Given a single observed sample, what is the center of the
    *boostrap distribution* of the sample mean?

    **Solution:** The sample mean is an *unbiased* estimator of the
    population mean. So the center of the sampling distribution of the
    sample mean should be equal to the true population mean.\
    \
    Given a single observed sample, that sample is treated as the
    population distribution for the population of bootstrap sampling. So
    the observed sample mean plays the role of the population mean for
    bootstrap sampling, and the bootstrap distribution will be centered
    at *the observed value of the statistic*.\

2.  Suppose we want to estimate the population SD? Is the sample SD an
    unbiased estimator of the population SD? Does this cause any issues
    for CIs?

    **Solution:** The sample variance is unbiased, but the sample SD is
    not: the sample SD tends to underestimate the population SD,
    $\textrm{E}(S) < \sigma$. The center of the bootstrap distribution
    with be the sample SD, which tends to underestimate the population
    SD. This introduces bias, and so the true coverage probability could
    be less than the stated confidence level. Bootstrap
    Normal/percentile intervals only account for sample-to-sample
    variability of the statistic, not bias.

3.  How could we use bootstrapping to estimate the bias of the sample SD
    (as an estimator of the population SD)?

    **Solution:** Given a single observed sample, the observed sample SD
    plays the role of the population SD for bootstrap sampling. *So bias
    can be estimated by comparing the center of the bootstrap
    distribution to the observed value of the statistic.*

    -   The bootstrap distribution of a statistic approximates many, but
        not all, features of the sampling distribution of the statistic.

        -   In particular, the center of the bootstrap distribution will
            generally not be the same as the center of the sampling
            distribution.

        -   This can lead to coverage problems (e.g., less than the
            stated 95%) for bootstrap percentile intervals, especially
            for statistics which are biased estimators of their
            parameters.

    -   Bootstrap percentile intervals do not fully account for
        differences between the observed statistic and the true
        parameter

    -   Remember, there are two sources of differences between a
        statistic and a corresponding parameter

        -   systematic errors due to *estimation bias*[^2]

        -   "chance errors" due to natural *sample-to-sample
            variability*

    -   The usual confidence procedures assume that there is no bias in
        estimation. The margin of error of a confidence interval
        typically only accounts for natural sample-to-sample
        variability. So if there is bias in estimation, the actual
        coverage probability of the confidence interval procedure might
        be less than the nominal confidence level.

    -   Recall that the bias of an estimator $\hat{\theta}$ of a
        parameter $\theta$ is $\textrm{E}(\hat{\theta}) - \theta$

        -   That is, the bias of an estimator is the difference between
            the center of its sampling distribution and the true (but
            unknown) value of the parameter

        -   If a statistic is *unbiased*, the center of its sampling
            distribution should be equal to the true (but unknown) value
            of the parameter.

    -   Bootstrapping treats the observed sample data as the population
        for the purposes of simulation. Therefore, bootstrapping treats
        the observed value of the statistic as the true value of the
        parameter for the purposes of simulation.

    -   If a statistic is an unbiased estimator of a parameter, the
        center of its bootstrap distribution should be equal to *the
        observed value of the statistic*.

    -   The difference between the center of the bootstrap distribution
        of the statistic and the observed value of the statistic
        provides a bootstrap estimate of the statistic's bias

    -   A *bootstrap pivotal confidence interval* essentially uses the
        distribution of $\hat{\theta}-\theta$, rather than just
        $\hat{\theta}$, to construct a confidence interval that more
        fully accounts for both bias and variability.

    -   The 95% **bootstrap pivotal confidence interval** is the
        interval with endpoints $$\begin{aligned}
            \text{lower endpoint} & = 2\times \text{observed statistic} - \text{97.5th percentile of bootstrap distribution}\\
            \text{upper endpoint} & = 2\times \text{observed statistic} - \text{2.5th percentile of bootstrap distribution}\\
        \end{aligned}$$

4.  Find a 95% bootstrap pivotal interval for the population mean.
    Compare to the percentile interval.

    **Solution:** The sample mean is 340. The 95% percentile interval is
    $[247, 443]$. The 95% pivotal interval is
    $$[2(340) - 443, 2(340) - 247] \Rightarrow [237, 433]$$ The two
    intervals are pretty similar.

5.  Find a 95% bootstrap pivotal interval for the population SD. Compare
    to the percentile interval.

    **Solution:** The sample SD is 145.6. The 95% percentile interval is
    $[52, 182]$. The 95% pivotal interval is
    $$[2(145.6) - 182, 2(145.6) - 52] \Rightarrow [109, 239]$$ There is
    a much bigger disparity in the two intervals for the population SD
    than for the population mean.

-   The accuracy of bootstrap procedures is primarily influenced by the
    size of the original sample.

-   Bootstrapping methods do not overcome the weaknesses of small
    samples.

[^1]: Source:
    <http://harrypotter.wikia.com/wiki/Inter-House_Quidditch_Cup>

[^2]: Of course there is also lots of potential for bias in data
    collection, but we always assume we have an unbiased random sample.
    Even when the data are a random sample from the population, there
    can still be bias in estimation.
